item.title: Oh Sure, NOW Nick Clegg Tells Tech Bros They Were Wrong To Back Trump
item.author: Mike Masnick
item.content:encoded: I’m getting a bit tired of the so-called “prodigal tech bros” who worked in tech companies, and only really speak out about the terrible decisions made by the leaders of those companies after they leave (at which point they get way more press coverage than anyone who has been criticizing those decisions all along). But this new piece from Nick Clegg in The Atlantic, saying that “Getting Too Close to Trump Was a Mistake“, feels like a new variation on the genre. Like the prodigal tech bros, his message isn’t necessarily wrong, just coming way too late from a messenger who should have actually taken a stand earlier.If you don’t recall, Nick Clegg is the former UK politician (and deputy Prime Minister) who then went to Facebook/Meta, where he spent a few years as their “President for Global Affairs” (effectively, second in command to Zuck) where he tended to be rolled out to take political heat for unpopular decisions. He was the one who made it clear that Zuck was willing to give up Section 230 to allow governments to “regulate” Facebook… in a manner that would harm Meta’s competitors way more than Meta.He left in January of 2025 as Trump’s second term was set to begin, allowing Joel Kaplan — who was way more connected to US GOP politics — to take his place. So, in some sense, it’s little surprise that Clegg is now willing to throw Trump under the bus. But also, a bit late for that, Nick. Some of us were calling this shit out right away, when it was still extremely politically inconvenient to do so, rather than waiting until after the American public spoke out loud and clear during the midterms.As for Clegg’s reasoning as to why Silicon Valley’s leaders lined up behind Trump, he’s right that they basically got none of what they hoped to get:First, tech leaders said that uniting the power of Washington and Silicon Valley would help America in its fight with China for AI supremacy. Yet over the past 18 months, China has been closing the gap with the United States by most objective measures, including model performance and chip development. In some important respects, China has outpaced America altogether, deploying open-weight models faster, developing a more sustainable energy strategy, and training world-class researchers and engineers at a larger scale.Second, Silicon Valley leaders said that partnering with the government would help assuage public concerns about AI and overcome the “woke” opposition to Big Tech. Yet societal attitudes toward AI in the U.S. are much more negative now than they ever were under President Biden, and worse than almost anywhere else on the planet. Fostering the very backlash they claimed they were trying to confront is a peculiar triumph of hubris and incompetence.Third, tech executives hoped that earning Trump’s good graces would allow them to avoid unwelcome regulatory incursions outside the U.S., especially in Europe. The Trump administration has undoubtedly helped with this in some ways. For example, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has become an important ally for tech leaders trying to fight a number of European Union enforcement decisions. But by any other meaningful measure the approach has been a disaster: Anti–Big Tech, and (alas) anti-American, sentiment has never been higher in large parts of the world, and most major economies—including Canada’s, India’s, Germany’s, and Brazil’s—are now scrambling to have less, not more, of what Silicon Valley produces.Since Silicon Valley pivoted to Trump, then, its scorecard has looked something like this:chief rival (China) strengthened; domestic support weakened; global markets infuriated.Again, though, there were plenty of people who warned about this as soon as they started up lining up behind Trump (even before the 2024 election). None of this was difficult to predict. So it seems a bit unseemly to bring all this up now.Clegg’s analysis of they missed it so much is at least a little bit more interesting. I’m not sure I agree with them all. His first one is that they had “FOMO” about Elon Musk’s close relationship with Trump, and were worried that this would undercut their own company’s efforts while competing with Musk’s companies. I don’t buy that FOMO alone explains it — the miscalculation seems so obvious that almost anyone could have seen it coming from the start.The more interesting one to me is this one:. Tech leaders had a lot to be angry about in the run-up to Trump’s reelection. Some felt unfairly treated by traditional media, academia, and cultural elites. Conservatives had long felt unwelcome in the Valley’s traditionally liberal milieu. The Biden administration had clumsily vilified tech leaders rather than work with them on policy and regulation. These factors created a large group of powerful, wealthy, and offended individuals. Stepping into the Trump tent seemed like a good way to even the score.I actually do think this was a major motivating factor among many (and have pointed that out a few times as well). But Clegg should point out how pathetic and silly this is. Tech leaders are some of the most powerful executives in the world. The fact that they got so offended that the Biden admin didn’t kiss their ass is no reason to throw in with fascism. This has nothing to do with high school popularity and cliques — it’s about having some fucking standards about humanity and basic rights.On the next point, though, I do think Clegg is spot on:Misunderstanding politics. As someone who spent nearly two decades in elected office and has spent much of my time since working in and around tech, I am always struck by how eagerly smart and wealthy people expound on subjects about which they know very little—especially politics. Their commercial success seems to foster in them a view that politics is easy, if only dim-witted officeholders would listen to them. It is this hubris that makes the Valley such an exhilarating and exasperating place.I don’t think this is necessarily limited to tech bros. Indeed, I don’t think it’s necessarily limited to the wealthy. Lots of people have very strong (often ill-informed) opinions on lots of things. The real problem is that with the ultra wealthy, people feel a ridiculous obligation to take their brain farts on other subjects seriously. That’s where the mistakes come in. This is compounded by the assumption that because tech bros create magical-seeming innovations, they must also have special insight into policy and the future. I’m as critical as anyone of politicians not understanding tech, but the same is true in the other direction, where people in tech tend to have a very confused and unrealistic understanding of politics.But a big part of the problem is that people take the stupid policy ideas from the tech bros seriously because of their wealth and the fact that they once lucked into selling some random business for hundreds of millions of dollars. And it seems like many of the tech bros assumed — incorrectly — that the public adulation they had received for years for their innovations would follow them into the realm of politics.The reality is the reverse has happened. As they’ve embraced fascism and Trumpism, rather than having the public come along with them, the public (especially younger people) no longer trust them at all. Embracing Trumpism completely burned bridges with young Americans:But again, this turn of events shouldn’t have been a surprise. Innovators were celebrated when they focused on making people’s lives better, and actually empowering them. But over the last decade, the leaders of the field, the same ones who lined up behind Donald Trump, seemed to totally ignore how the public’s views regarding their own platforms had shifted. And that’s because they had shifted from an era of actually empowering people to one of extracting as much as they could from them, and then demanding more.The innovations no longer seemed cool and interesting and empowering. They seemed needy and aggressive and extractive.Clegg’s piece is frustrating in that there are elements of it that are absolutely accurate. But it comes way too late and in too weak a form. As I said right after the election, much of Silicon Valley is actually working on unique and useful innovations and doesn’t support the fascist MAGA project. But too many of the CEOs and the VCs decided to buy in, and now they’re going to face blowback. My fear is that the blowback directed at the shitty leaders of shitty companies will actually do more damage to the underlying internet that people still rely on, rather than just narrowly targeting the actual bad actors.While Clegg admits that Democrats in Congress are likely to investigate the tech industry for their coziness with Trump, he misses the larger point: the blast radius of those investigations will go beyond just those companies that embraced what they thought was a fascist cheat code to dominance. It’s going to make it much harder for the actual innovation, the smaller companies, and the new services that actually empower people, to exist as well. The end result is going to be a lockdown on the wider industry, because a few shithead leaders of the biggest companies couldn’t think just a few steps into the future.There’s real collateral damage from the tech bros’ embrace of fascism, and avoiding it starts with not sugarcoating what a mess this was all along — and discussing directly how much damage their embrace of Trumpist fascism will do to the good parts of the internet.

item.title: Gamers Skip Work to Play GTA VI After 13-Year Wait

After a 13-year wait, Rockstar games' Grand Theft Auto VI has officially (and finally) launched today to near-universal acclaim, earning a 99/100 score on Metacritic and generating an estimated $1.84 billion from 19 million copies sold. The highly anticipated release has prompted gamers to take time off work, attracted nearly 2 million concurrent Twitch viewers, and sparked celebrations around the world. An expert told Reuters that there could be a "work blackout across the board." Another expert suggested that $1 billion in U.S. productivity could be lost as people take time off to play the game, which is estimated to take about 50 hours to complete.
Here's a roundup of GTA VI reviews:
IGN (10/10) calls it "the single most impressive video game I have ever played." GameSpot (10/10) praises its extraordinary attention to detail, calling it a culmination of Rockstar's open-world achievements. Push Square (10/10) describes it as Rockstar's deepest and most accomplished open world since Red Dead Redemption 2, though it notes the 30fps cap and occasional pacing issues. Eurogamer (5/5) praises its ambitious world and the emotional depth of Jason and Lucia's relationship. Digital Foundry highlights its groundbreaking visual realism, ray tracing, and simulation detail, while acknowledging compromises from the 30fps target. Bloomberg calls it an all-time classic, praising the unpredictable interactions and remarkable freedom of exploration.

item.title: Microsoft Testing Remote Lock For Lost Or Stolen Windows Devices
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
joshuark quotes a report from BleepingComputer: Microsoft is testing a new feature that lets enterprise IT administrators remotely lock stolen or lost Windows devices without wiping them. Named Remote Lock, this new feature is shipping to devices upgraded to Windows 11 Insider Preview builds in the Beta (Build 26320.10003) and Experimental (Build 26340.10013) channels.
Admins can use Microsoft Intune custom configuration profiles to lock Microsoft Entra-joined, hybrid-joined, or MDM-enrolled devices that run Windows Enterprise, Education, or Pro. After the IT department remotely locks the device, the system can only be unlocked via Intune, since PINs, passwords, local admins, or web sign-ins will no longer work. Microsoft added that the user's credentials will remain valid and can still be used to sign into other devices that haven't been locked. "Windows signs out every active session, hides all sign-in options and shows a locked screen," said Windows Insider communications lead Stephen Lines. "Nothing is erased: the device stays enrolled and managed, BitLocker stays on and user data stays in place. The lock holds across restarts and while offline, and only an admin can lift it remotely, so the user picks up where they left off."

item.title: High-End Furniture Marketplace AptDeco Is Taking People’s Furniture and Not Paying Them
item.author: Jason Koebler
item.content:encoded: This article has been updated with comment from AptDeco.Last month, Erin sold a $3,000 large designer table on AptDeco, a white glove high-end furniture marketplace. More than a month later, she feels like she’s been literally robbed.“AptDeco sent three men to physically collect my table on October 13, and here we are on November 16, with no payment and no concrete explanation for where my $2,000 (after their absurd $900 fee) is,” Erin told me. “It genuinely feels like I’ve had something stolen from me.”AptDeco is a Y Combinator-backed company whose entire purpose is to take the risk out of places like Facebook Marketplace and Craigslist for designer furniture resale. It advertises itself as “simple and seamless,” and says “we handle pickup, delivery, and payments,” and claims that it pays sellers “within 5-10 business days.” But over the last few months, people who have sold furniture on the platform say that AptDeco has sold their furniture and taken it from their houses, but hasn’t paid them. 404 Media agreed to only use Erin’s first name because she is still trying to get her money from the company.“Adding to the chorus of people who sold an item thru AptDeco and never received payment. I have no idea what to do at this point,” another says. “Can we do a class action lawsuit?” another reads.“They owed me money since September 30th,” a fourth says. Every recent review and complaint on AptDeco’s Better Business Bureau page is from sellers who have not been paid: “Almost 6 weeks after they picked up and not being paid Pick up was a nightmare too No calls nobody doing anything Do NOT SELL ON APTDECO,” one reads. Another states “I have been in an endless loop with customer service for 2 months trying to get my payout for the bed I sold. I am losing faith that I will ever see this money. Extremely frustrated at this experience.”On AptDeco’s website, everything appears to be business as usual. You can still buy and sell furniture, and there is no indication of anything wrong at all. 404 Media’s repeated attempts to reach AptDeco to ask what was going on went unreturned.In communications with sellers seen by 404 Media, AptDeco’s customer service representatives have repeatedly blamed their payment processor, a “technical bug,” or have said the payment is “moving through the system.” On November 3, AptDeco told Erin that a bug had prevented her from being paid, that the payment team “retried” it, and that she would be paid within 10 days. “I’ve asked our team to prioritize your payout personally, so you should see it in your bank account by then - hopefully sooner! At this point, we’re doing everything we can to get your payout processed,” a customer support email reviewed by 404 Media reads. On Tuesday, two weeks after the company told her the payment had been retried, a different customer service representative followed up and said “I'm truly sorry — I know this isn't the update you were hoping for. Your payout is still being prioritized by our payments team, and I want to be honest with you: I don't yet have a confirmed release date or timeline to share.”Several other people who have sold items on AptDeco recently told 404 Media they’re experiencing the same problem.Harry Heymann sold a Room & Board couch on AptDeco in late September and still has not been paid the $120 he is owed by the platform. The messages he’s gotten from AptDeco customer support read much the same as Erin’s: They claim “a technical bug on our end held up your payout” and the customer service representative said “I’ve asked our team to prioritize your payout personally.” Late last week, he got what reads like an AI-generated message that reads “I know how frustrating this has been. You've been waiting on your $120 payout, the date you were given has passed, and you've had to follow up to get answers. That's not the experience we want for you, and I'm truly sorry. Your case has been escalated to me, and l'm happy to be your point of contact from here. Unfortunately, the issue with our payment processor has not yet been resolved, and our team is still working on it.” Natalie Simmons sold an armoire in late August and told 404 Media she initially had a good experience compared to using other platforms. But then she never got her money. “After so many uncomfortable situations on different social sites I was so happy when I found AptDeco,” she told me. “I received notification that my payment would arrive in 3-5 business days through the portal in app. That was Aug 30th. I tried calling but the voicemail says leave a message and they will respond by email. I emailed several times and finally after 2 weeks and a few voicemails I received an email that there was a glitch with their payment system and I will receive payment within 5-10 business days. After another 2 weeks I called and emailed again that I still didn’t receive payment. They sent another email with the exact same story. I just want to get paid. It’s not even that much but it’s the principle.”It’s not just sellers who have had issues with the platform. One customer, K Turner, bought a couch and tried to return it. Rather than giving her a refund, the company said they would relist it at the price she paid and then give her a “refund” of whatever it sold for minus fees. The couch resold quickly at the beginning of September and the company told her she would quickly get her “refund.” More than a month later, on October 20, they told her “I have gone ahead and processed that refund ($600) manually. Please allow 5-10 business days for this refund to be reflected back to your original form of payment.” She has still not gotten her money. “The communication was decent at first, but once they confirmed the item resold on September 8th, they then went silent. It took me a month to finally get a response. They confirmed that the item resold at the full listing price of $600 and that I would receive my refund to my original payment in 5 - 10 business days,” Turner told me. “That was nearly a month ago, and I still don't have my money. So, they effectively double-dipped. They got my money from the original order and then collected money by reselling it. And who knows if they ever gave the money to the original seller; maybe they triple-dipped. I have threatened legal action twice now.”The customers I spoke to have no idea what happens next. Some of them said they were going to file claims in small claims court or are considering a class action lawsuit. But the company is mostly giving them what appear to be canned, copy-pasted statements that come from a revolving cast of customer support email addresses, and no actual updates. Four emails from 404 Media asking for comment, including emails sent to the company’s CEO, have not been returned. AptDeco promises a high-end, safe experience when compared to somewhere like Facebook Marketplace or Craigslist, and markets itself primarily for more expensive, lightly-used furniture. The people I spoke to said they wish they had just stayed off the platform altogether.“The irony is that I’m now feeling safer selling expensive designer furniture directly to strangers on Facebook Marketplace than through a platform whose entire purpose is supposedly to make these transactions safer and more secure,” Erin said. “At this point, AptDeco has my furniture, I have no money, and I’m left chasing them for something I’m already owed. It’s an incredibly unsettling position to be in, particularly when so many other sellers seem to be experiencing the same thing. The fact that I continue to receive email marketing newsletters and see them selling via Google Ads—paying that platform before their sellers—is infuriating.”After this article was published (and three days after we initially asked for comment), an AptDeco spokesperson gave 404 Media a convoluted explanation involving “bot swarms,” which it blamed for the delays in seller payouts. “Over the past few months, we’ve been dealing with an unprecedented volume of bot activity, some of it malicious. This has created a myriad of challenges that we’ve been actively working to address.These bot swarms, along with the broader cybersecurity challenges of an AI-evolving world, prompted us to significantly strengthen our site’s security to ensure the long-term protection of our buyers and sellers,” the spokesperson said. “To be clear, customer data has not been compromised in any way. However, we’ve been investing heavily in preventative measures to further protect our community. Unfortunately, some of these efforts have resulted in delays in seller payouts. As you can imagine, cybersecurity is a complex and sensitive topic, making it challenging to communicate all the details broadly. That said, the issue has now been resolved, and outstanding payouts are being processed. Any seller with questions can email and will hear back within 1 business day. We appreciate your patience and understanding.”When I asked for clarification because it was not clear how bot swarms would affect payouts, the spokesperson said “the bot swarm did not affect seller payouts.”“We deployed code to further improve protections for our customers (given the bot swarms) which inadvertently impacted seller payout processing. Providing additional technical context would require a detailed understanding of our codebase and would likely be more information than is relevant or useful to readers,” they added. “That said, we sincerely apologize to our customers for the delays and are committed to making things right. The issue has been resolved, our security infrastructure remains extremely robust, and outstanding payouts are being processed. We appreciate you reaching out and giving us the opportunity to clarify. This will be our final comment on the matter.”also pointed out that the company is being sued by American Express for allegedly failing to pay a $158,461 credit card bill from 2024; that case is in default judgment but is ongoing.

item.title: Black Neighborhoods Are Twice as Likely To House a Data Center, Study Finds
item.author: Matthew Gault
item.content:encoded: Developers build data centers in communities of color at more than twice the rate they do in white neighborhoods, according to a new study from researchers at George Washington University and the Center for Security, Innovation & New Technology (CSINT) at American University.According to the study, “Redlining in the Age of AI: The Relationship between Data Center Locations and Race in the US” majority-Black neighborhoods have 2.2 times the odds of hosting a data center than a white neighborhood in the same state. The number goes up to 2.6 in majority-Hispanic neighborhoods and 4.2 times in majority-Asian neighborhoods. “As the share of Black, Hispanic, and Asian residents in a neighborhood increases, so do the odds that the neighborhood hosts a data center,” the researchers wrote.The researchers ran the numbers by examining 81,000 US census tracts and location data for 5,291 data centers. “We found that these racial disparities persist even after accounting for factors such as population, household income, education, land costs, proximity to major transmission lines, and state fixed effects,” they wrote. “These results hold even though data centers are concentrated in and around metropolitan areas, which are often more racially diverse.”“We really wanted to look at this on a nationwide scale to see: is this something that fits into this broader structural racism story?” CSINT executive director Samantha Bradshaw told 404 Media. “What we did find was yes [...] neighborhoods that have data centers tend to have a higher ratio of people of color.”Bradshaw and co-author Dhanaraj Thakur told 404 Media that they were inspired to do the study after reading stories about data centers in Memphis, Tennessee polluting Black and Brown communities. Another high profile case occurred in Taylor, Texas where a white family donated a tract of land to the city with the intention it become a public part. That land abutted a Black neighborhood. The city never built a park there and now it’s slated to become a data centerAccording to the researchers, the historical legacy of — the process of denying Americans of color loans and other opportunities to keep them in specific neighborhoods — is to blame for some of this. Data centers are often built near transmission lines because they provide ease of access to power infrastructure, for example. Those transmission lines were often built in majority Black neighborhoods in America. Thakur said he doubted that data centers developers were seeking to intentionally put data centers in communities of color. “It’s just how embedded race is with all these other factors,” he said. The study distinguished between several different kinds of data centers and noted there are massive differences between hyperscalers like what Meta, Google, and Grok are building and smaller mixed use buildings that often serve as network transmission hubs as well as compute warehouses, which the study called “co-location facilities.” When a hyperscaler comes to town, the developers sometimes promise economic investment in the community where it’s being constructed and those facilities typically aren’t built in communities of color..Meta is building a $50 billion data center in rural Louisiana. Community leaders there have said it would bring 1,000 permanent jobs and that sales tax revenues have already jumped 2,000 percent, leading to a $50,000 bonus for area teachers. Even here, there is disparity. Most of the hyperscalers that promise massive economic benefits to local communities are built in white rural communities. The study makes several suggestions about what to do about all this including data center-specific zoning regulations, prioritizing racial equity in discussions around building them, and requiring racial impact statements for data centers before they’re built. Thakur and Bradshaw emphasized that tech policy should be a negotiation between the companies that provide the tech and the communities that use it. Data centers have spurred these conversations — they’re physical representations of Big Tech’s powers, a power that Americans recently rejected at the ballot box. “AI has a physical geography, and that geography is shaped by political and social history,” the researchers wrote in the study.“I think the issue around how racial justice, civil rights plays into many other kinds of policies —health, education, housing, whatever it is — we just don't see enough of that consideration in tech policy, and I think this this kind of analysis shows why this that why we should be doing that, thinking about that more,” Thakur said.Bradshaw agreed. “If you look at who's represented in tech policy and who built these systems, who designs them, who engineers them, it's a very specific kind of white male Silicon Valley California ideology engineer, and that is not representative of the technology and its users,” she said. “So I think bringing in these perspectives is really really important because then we can truly think about ways to design a tech future that is for everybody.

item.title: ICE Is Paying AT&T to Dig Through a Mountain of Call Records
item.author: Joseph Cox
item.content:encoded: This article was primarily reported using public records requests. We are making it available to all readers as a public service. FOIA reporting can be expensive, please consider subscribing to 404 Media to support this work. Or send us a one time donation via our tip jar here.Immigration and Customs Enforcement is paying telecommunications giant AT&T millions of dollars to have AT&T’s analysts sift through mountains of raw AT&T data for a wide variety of investigations, according to an internal ICE document obtained by 404 Media, other procurement records, and experts who reviewed those records. Civil liberty experts have called it a mass surveillance program, and they say the data can include trillions of phone records and location data. The AT&T product, interchangeably called Data Analytics and Support Services or Data Analytical Services, appears to be related to an earlier surveillance program called Hemisphere, in which AT&T provided U.S. authorities at state, local, and federal levels access to AT&T user data. Though that program shut down, ICE is still paying for access to raw data under this new arrangement with AT&T, according to the restricted ICE procurement document obtained by 404 Media. The program likely affects more than just AT&T customers because the company connects phone calls for other phone companies, meaning non-customers are likely swept up too, according to a surveillance expert.“This requirement provides ICE access to AT&T’s raw data and experienced analysts,” the document obtained by 404 Media reads.Do you know anything else about this data? Do you work at ICE or another federal agency using it? I would love to hear from you. Using a non-work device, you can message me securely on Signal at joseph.404 or send me an email at joseph@404media.co.AT&T told 404 Media the data is made available under a valid legal order, but experts point out it requires an administrative subpoena, which agencies can issue themselves and don’t require a judge’s approval, raising concerns that ICE can use the data for essentially whatever it wants. The document also shows how financial incentives play a part in providing data to ICE.

item.title: Charting American Culture in News Footage of ‘Grand Theft Auto’
item.author: Matthew Gault
item.content:encoded: Some people spent the week leading up to the release of replaying the old games. I, sicko that I am, spent it watching TV news coverage of the franchise from the past 20 years.Grand Theft Auto has been a staple of cable and broadcast TV news since at least the release of in 2001. I’ve been an adult for all of it; I’ve had a front row seat for two decades of moral panics, parental freakouts, and bizarre political theater. The games and the broader culture’s reaction to them have changed dramatically in that time. In 2001, newscasters worried GTA III was training an army of young men to kill. In 2026, earnestly quoted Bell Hooks in its review of GTA VI.For mainstream news, GTA is the ur-video game. The open world that mirrors our own, the prevalence of sex and death, and the increasingly realistic simulations and graphics pointed towards the dream of what a video game could be. GTA is the American id made manifest.You can chart America’s changing culture — especially its anxieties — by watching how the media covered Grand Theft Auto. This was, at first, the game that critics of the medium had always warned us about: a violent sex and death simulator that rotted the brains of the youth just as rock and roll and comics had done in ages past. Twenty years on, the brains are thoroughly rotted, GTA won, and now? Now we’re all worried about money.GTA III and — Murder Simulators, the Assassin of YouthRockstar released in October 2001 and just a year later. The controversy around both started right away and centered around violence, and sometimes, the game’s depiction of women. “This is the world’s most popular video game [...] and millions of kids are mastering it by learning to slaughter bystanders,” Ted Koppel told America.Nightline devoted 20 minutes of its broadcast to GTA in July 2002. It interviewed children who grinned ear to ear as they gunned down people in GTA, their parents who insisted it was just a game, a concerned expert who was sure GTA was training them to kill, and a psychologist who said that was bullshit. It all ended with a roundtable discussion where a police officer, in uniform, explained the differences between video games and real world violence.Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas — Congressional Hearings and Sex on TVI was an assistant manager of a Gamestop in Texas in 2004 when Rockstar released Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas. The level of parental concern in the store was high in the weeks leading up to its release. One mother was so upset by a bearing a cover story about that she told me I was going to hell for “selling a gangster lifestyle” to children.But it was sex, not violence, that the news focused on with . The game had a lot of simulation elements — its protagonist would gain weight if he ate too much — and Rockstar had experimented with a sex minigame called “hot coffee.” Developers cut the minigame from the final release, but it was still on the physical discs that went to stores. Modders uncovered it in the files and were able to patch it back in.California politician Leland Yee got wind of the mod and condemned the Entertainment Software Ratings Board (ESRB) for labeling the game “Mature” instead of “Adults Only.” Cable news went wild. Rachel Maddow weighed in. Hillary Clinton, then a Senator in New York, demanded an investigation. Congress voted to send the FTC after Rockstar for deceiving the ESRB. The ESRB updated the game’s rating to an AO. Walmart, Best Buy, and other retailers . publisher Take-Two shipped new copies with the content completely removed. Take-Two’s shareholders also removed most of its board and put Strauss Zelnick in charge. He’s been the CEO ever since.— The Ballad of Jack ThompsonThe cultural winds had shifted by the time hit stores in 2008. Retailers across the country had midnight release parties where people lined up to purchase the game as soon as possible. Local news outlets interviewed people in line and marveled at how much money might make.But the culture warriors still pointed to GTA as proof of America’s moral decline. Glenn Beck, then an anchor on CNN Headline News, on the game and often spoke to American lawyer Jack Thompson. Thompson hated Grand Theft Auto so much and was so sure it was training young people to kill their elders that he let his crusade against the franchise ruin his life.Thompson against Take-Two aimed at preventing the company from selling at all. The publisher counter-sued, Thompson accused it of perjury, and the parties eventually settled. In its ruling, the courts said Thompson could never use the legal system to stop Take-Two from publishing a game ever again.He didn’t stop though. After the game came out, Thompson Rockstar had based an assassination mission on him. He then sent a letter to Strauss Zelnick’s mom. “Your son, this very moment, is doing everything he possibly can to sell as many copies of GTA IV to teen boys in the United States, a country in which your son claims you raised him to be ‘a Boy Scout.’ More like the Hitler Youth, I would say. Happy Mother’s day, Mrs. Zelnick, which this year is May 11, two weeks after your son unleashes porn and violence upon other mothers’ boys. I'm sure you’re very proud,” Thompson wrote in the letter.The Supreme Court of Florida permanently disbarred him shortly thereafter.Money in the Age of ViolenceIn 2013, made a billion dollars in three days and was the biggest entertainment release of all time. It made more money than any movie, book, album, or video game had ever made before. Every news broadcast about the game led with that fact. “Never has there been an opening like this in the entertainment industry,” CBS News said.Jake Tapper and CNET’s Dan Ackerman lamented that GTA V’s success would hurt the creativity of the video game industry. “It’s become such a hit-driven business. You have to have a big opening day or opening weekend for anyone to take you seriously. And when you have such a hit-driven business, I think people get risk averse and they don’t get as creative,” Ackerman told Tapper. The news still ran segments about the violence and sex in the game, but it was typically couched in a conversation about its runaway financial success. Most anchors brought on experts who told them about the business. They sought to understand what was happening and why people liked the game, rather than condemning it outright. Anxieties of American DeclineIn 2026, cultural fears about violence and sex in video games are gone. Instead, we’re all worried about money. Everyone is sure will make money, the question is if it will make the money?“Why the stakes for GTA VI are so high,” declared the thumbnail for a Bloomberg video about the game. The outlet’s podcast also ran an episode about why the . Newsweek worried that the U.S. economy as people take time off work to play. CBS News’ morning show wondered how much money the game would make and the anchor admitted he once “lost a summer” to Grand Theft Auto. No one discussed violence at all. CNBC’s coverage called the game a “Billion Dollar Hype Machine.”Behind it all is a kind of lament — a worry that might be a final hurrah for this kind of game. Rumors are that it cost a billion dollars. Games are more expensive than ever and the industry has been devastated. A third of the industry lost their jobs in the past 24 months and most of them . Even when a game is successful, companies cut staff. wondered if GTA VI “may be the last great heist.”Underneath all these economic fears, the older panics still lurked. On Fox News, middling collegiate swimmer turned political activist Riley Gaines hoped that the game’s romantic elements would lead to a rise in birth rates. “Hopefully these men realize they like the feeling of love, romantic love, and go out and find it. Because, I’ll tell you what, we’re in a population decline. We need more babies. You can’t have babies, real babies, mouths to feed, from video games,” Gaines said.Twitch streamer Sasha Grey had early access to the game and was streaming it to YouTube and Twitch when YouTube shut down her stream for “nudity.” An early cutscene showed what Grey described as “artistic nip and some booty.” Grey complained to YouTube in a post on X and shared a screenshot of the moment the company shut down her stream. “They allow far worse under their educational category. This game is art, y’know? It’s the biggest release of the friggin’ decade,” Grey said during her stream. She pulled up the post on X to see if she’d gotten a response. “Oh god, the Twitter post got labeled as adult content, which means it’s going to be harder to get seen.”The old protestant advertiser-friendly anti-sex morality is still there, programmed into the computer systems we use every day.

AI is integral to the world of computer science. Software engineering remains one of the largest professional job categories, and employers now expect software engineers to be fluent in AI. The AP Exam includes free-response questions about the project, so students who earn a qualifying score for college credit have demonstrated their ability to design, build, and understand an AI-powered application. [...] Students need access to a district-approved AI tool that accepts a student's own written instructions and returns a response. Schools will need to make sure every student has access to one."
The College Board also announced a planned ban on the use of block-based programming languages like Snap!, Scratch, Blockly, and MIT App Inventor for students' "AI Create Project" (which replaces the current "Create Performance Task" that counts for 30% of a student's AP exam score): "Beginning with the 2028-29 school year, students will submit their AI Create Project in one of a limited number of text-based languages. This change aligns the course with introductory college computer science courses, where text-based languages are most commonly used. If you currently teach programming with block-based tools, you can continue to use them in your teaching while introducing text-based languages throughout the year. Students will need to be working in an approved text-based language by the time they submit their AI Create Project in 2028-29."

item.title: Satellites Now Outnumber the Visible Stars Above Most Towns
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Satellites now outnumber visible stars in the night sky above many towns and cities, according to a non-peer-reviewed analysis by engineering firm Accu Components. The researchers estimated that roughly 710 satellites pass over an average U.K. town at any given moment, with about 105 illuminated by sunlight and potentially visible to the naked eye. Space.com reports: Although the researchers specifically focused on the U.K., they say that such heavy satellite traffic flows above most of Europe, the U.S. and other mid-latitude regions, especially between 40 and 50 degrees north or south. "Most Starlink satellites orbit at around 53 degrees to the equator, so the satellites bunch up over the mid-latitudes. These worldwide figures are approximate, based on a global grid over a single day," Accu Components spokesperson told Space.com in an email. "Skies near the equator are the quietest, with around 490 satellites."
Not all of those satellites are visible to the naked eye, the researchers said in a statement. Because satellites unlike stars don't produce their own light, they must be illuminated by the sun, while the ground below has already sunk into darkness, to be visible. [...] The spokesperson said that the actual number of visible satellites varies drastically throughout the night. During the hours after dusk and before dawn, a much greater number of satellites can be seen, while in the middle of the night most no longer catch any light. "For a typical U.K. town, around 300 satellites are catching the sunlight in the first hour or so after dark," the spokesperson said. "That falls to fewer than 20 around midnight, then climbs back to around 300 before dawn." [...] The study found that throughout the night, an average U.K. town sees 12,891 different satellites passing overhead.

item.title: America Loses Measles Elimination Status As Death Toll Rises To 10
item.author: Timothy Geigner
item.content:encoded: As America’s measles crisis continues to rage on, and even ramp up, we discussed recently that international health groups would be meeting this week to decide if the country will lose its measles elimination status. Thanks to the federal government’s complete failure to act on this crisis, the outcome of that meeting always seemed like a foregone conclusion. In the days since publishing that post, two things have happened: word leaked that the WHO would in fact rescind the elimination status for measles and the death toll from measles this year rose to 10. First, the embarrassment that is our loss of status. With outbreaks that have been smoldering and flaring since last year, the US has reportedly lost its measles elimination status—as medical and public health experts have widely expected it would. A panel of experts for the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), a regional branch of the World Health Organization, convened last week to review US measles data and assess its elimination status. The PAHO is set to announce its conclusion and the review’s other findings on Tuesday, November 17. But sources broke the news to The Wall Street Journal on Friday that the panel had found that the US had indeed lost its status.The US earned its elimination status in 2000 after hard-fought vaccination campaigns over several decades. But US vaccination rates have slipped below protective levels in recent years, fueled by the rise of anti-vaccine rhetoric and vaccine misinformation from fierce anti-vaccine advocates, including current US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. As vaccination rates slipped, measles cases skyrocketed. The current case tally is the highest seen since 1991.While this is unsurprising, it’s still painful to witness the country take such a massive and preventable step backwards in public health. Putting the anti-vaxxers in charge is how you get the return of measles. Putting the anti-vaxxer’s scion in charge of the nation’s health is how you get more people sick. And doing all of the above is how you get more people dying of diseases that could have been easily prevented with collective action to achieve herd immunity.In reporting the PAHO’s determination, the Journal quoted Noel Brewer, chair of an independent US committee who presented findings about the country’s measles outbreaks to PAHO, on the country’s lamentable status: “Runaway measles outbreaks in the United States, as well as the needless deaths, are all due to low measles vaccination coverage. We’ve gotten comfortable letting children be stopped by a deadly disease and die from it.”Just…let that sink in for a moment. We are not doing anything at the level of the federal government about the measles situation in America because we’ve gotten “comfortable” with children, some of them too young to be vaccinated even if their parents wanted them to be, getting sick and dying.There’s a lot to be angry about in our current state in America. A lot. But sick and dying children sure should be at the forefront of that anger. Appointing Kennedy as HHS Secretary is a mistake so obvious it barely needs stating. But what was Kennedy’s reaction to the GOP’s historic midterm loss? How is he dealing with the announcement that Stephen Miller would be taking over as Trump’s Chief of Staff?Miller, a right-wing hardliner, and Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the Trump administration’s unconventional health and human services secretary, met last week for dinner with their wives at the Millers’ home. There, Miller reportedly made a “radical” promise to RFK Jr., which the Kennedy scion later divulged to a room of Make America Healthy Again activists.“During that dinner, [Miller] said to me, ‘I’m the only one in the administration who’s more radical than you are on MAHA,'” Kennedy said at an event hosted by the advocacy group MAHA Action, according to The Washington Post.Kennedy celebrated Miller’s promotion and Susie Wiles’ ouster, declaring on social media: “Next to me, Stephen Miller is the strongest MAHA supporter in the administration. It’s time to unleash the Kraken.”These cretins are somehow, in the shadow of tiny little funeral caskets being lowered into the ground alongside children that died from a preventable disease, pledging to . Kennedy is so maniacally sociopathic that he can’t handle being wrong and must double down on his bullshit beliefs and policies. What Miller is up to is anyone’s guess, though it’s not hard to believe that a shared belief in eugenics with Kennedy has something to do with it. But these are just two men. Horrible, terrible men, to be sure, but just two men. They only get away with this if we let them. Don’t. Don’t let them. No more children should die from measles.

item.title: New Study Shows How Young People Feel About AI Companions
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from 404 Media: A new study from Gallup looked at how young people across the world are making friends, both digitally and in person. The good news is that around 93% of the young people surveyed reported having at least one strong in-person friendship. The weird news is that 33% said they had an AI companion. Gallup's study is lengthy and nuanced. It partnered with the Boston Children's Digital Wellness Lab to conduct the study and used online surveys of more than 16,000 young people from the ages of 15 to 22 in 16 different countries. A lot of the topline results won't surprise anyone living in today's constantly online digital-forward age. Gallup found that respondents felt their in-person friendships were their strongest, that digital friendships complemented rather than replaced in-person ones, and that stronger friendships made people happier no matter how the connection was made. Three things that stood out were how the young respondents talked about AI, loneliness, and doomscrolling.
Young people in the United States, Canada, and UK reported the least interest in AI overall, with only 20% saying they used it once a day or more. Almost 40 percent of young people in Brazil use it daily. Japan and Italy both come in around 35%. "Nearly half of young people in the United States, United Kingdom and Canada have used AI no more than a few times in the past month, including those who have not used it at all," the researchers wrote. Most of the respondents (82%) said they'd used AI to look up information, 68% asked it for advice, and 33% used it as a companion. Young people with online-only friends were more likely to use AI for companionship, "although these patterns do not establish whether AI companionship supplements or substitutes for human relationships," they wrote.
The researchers discovered that people in different countries felt wildly different about their AI buddies. Almost half of Australians with AI friends rated the relationship as "high quality" and only 12% of young people in Poland did. Mostly, though, people thought of their AI friends as mid: "In most countries [...] young people are more likely to give their AI companionship a medium rating than either a high or low rating." People who used AI as a friend also reported higher levels of loneliness, the study found. "However, the findings cannot determine whether young people turn to AI because they feel lonely, whether AI companionship influences their social experiences or whether other circumstances help explain these relationships," the researchers wrote. [...] The study's authors warned about reading too much into these results. "These assessments should be compared cautiously with those for human friendships examined in this report, as young people may have different expectations of what makes an AI companion or human friendship meaningful or supportive," the researchers wrote.
"The broader message is not that one form of connection is inherently better or worse, but that the quality of young people's relationships and the wider social context in which they exist matter greatly," the study concluded.

item.title: Can You Regulate ‘Fairness’? The EU’s Digital Fairness Act Is Going To Try
item.author: Mike Masnick
item.content:encoded: Last week the EU presented its long-awaited “Digital Fairness Act” proposal, an attempt to expand its consumer protection laws to deal with what it believes are shady practices online. Now, you might be thinking that the EU already has a ton of internet laws — the GDPR, the ePrivacy Directive, the DSA, the DMA, the AI Act, and more — with somewhat mixed results. And you’d be right. But that’s not going to slow down the EU.Dealing with scammy practices online is a laudable goal, but there are a lot of ways that could go wrong, especially if the end result is just giving more control to the biggest companies to “get things right” rather than letting users themselves control their own data and experiences online.As with many EU proposals, there’s a lot in this proposal that will likely get support, because it targets a bunch of things that people claim to hate. And, some of what the Commission lays out actually looks good:A ban on manipulative marketing tactics”) such as fake claims that a product is almost sold out that pressure consumers into purchasing decisions they might not otherwise make.Clear and transparent pricingparticularly prices of purchases made with virtual in-app currencies and when dynamic pricing is used for cultural and sports events. In virtual queues, companies will have to show the current price in real time and the highest possible price.with the option for consumersaddictive design featuresthat encourage excessive or compulsive spending, such as persistent prompts. The proposal will alsopractices that encourage overspending, for example by banning gambling-like features for minors, such as pay-to-win and pay-to-progress.Clear disclosure of influencer marketing, requiring influencers to be transparent about commercial content and preventing the exploitation of the trust of minors in their audience.A restriction on unfair personalised ads and prices that target minors or take advantage of sensitive dataDigital contracts and subscriptions that are easier to canceland an end to unwanted automatic renewals and free trials turning into subscription traps. Consumers will have the right to communicate with a human in customer service and will have clear rights when using an AI agent to buy products on their behalf.The key aspect of the proposal — and this is the subject of a lot of debate on both sides — is that it won’t most of the so-called “addictive” features (though it does ban a specific list of so-called “dark patterns”) but would require companies to give consumers the option of turning those features off. To me, that’s better than an outright ban, which would create lots of issues, but others complain that this then puts the burden on the user. Of course, one person’s “burden on the user” is another’s “user empowerment,” so it depends a bit on through which prism you view all this. I’d rather put control in users’ hands than give companies more levers to pull.Giving people the option to turn off these features actually seems like a mostly reasonable compromise. Many of the practices described above… absolutely suck. And being able to opt out of them seems good, though the devil is very much in the details. And some of the features being targeted can actually be useful in certain circumstances. I’ve talked about how the claims of “addictive design” are often quite overblown — mainly in confusing “addiction” and “habits.”And that can become problematic, because in addition to bad habits, there can also be habits — and there are even specialized tools out there designed to help you learn good habits, like getting regular exercise, or practicing mindfulness, or getting a good night’s sleep. Just as an example, Wired notes that a language-learning service like Duolingo or an exercise app like Strava might both be negatively impacted by the law. Both apps rely on features (like Duolingo’s infamous streaks) that nudge you to keep up with your language-learning and exercise habits. And, generally speaking, most people consider that a good thing. If it remains optional to turn these features off, then I guess that’s fine, though it still feels out of place in apps literally designed to try to get you to establish a habit (not an “addiction.”) At the very least, it will require they spend a bunch of engineering time to build a tool to turn off the main reason why people use those apps.But also, what starts as an “option” to turn off can quickly become required under the law. Indeed, some of the complaints about the proposal that we’re seeing are that many wish there were outright bans, rather than the option to turn off. Of course, in that same article, others are complaining that the existing rules are already too much of a regulatory burden, so you can see there will be efforts to pull the proposal in both directions as the negotiations between the European Parliament and the Council heat up over the final rules.The group EDRi, who does amazingly good consumer digital rights work in the EU, is largely supportive of the EU’s push to stop anti-consumer tricks online, but warns that the way the law is written might just create a repeat of the “cookie banner” nonsense, which was written to deal with a legitimate concern (people giving up privacy without realizing what they were doing) but when it came to implementation, resulted in just… annoying everyone and doing little to actually protect privacy.There is also a too familiar political risk: we’ve spent years watching companies turn cookie consent from a perfectly valid legal and protective basis into an obstacle course, only for the resulting frustration to become an argument against EU privacy and data protection regulation.There are also bits in the proposal targeting video game “loot boxes” and “pay-to-win” features, which… definitely feel more scammy. The proposal seeks to ban them in games targeted at children and provide much more clear transparency about what’s going on for adult gamers. Of course, the video game industry is already out complaining about these rules, but given how much of the world has been taken over by subtle attempts to make people gamble away everything they have… I’m not as convinced that rules on those kinds of things are as problematic as the industry makes them out to be.It also looks like the proposal did not take up the request to include the “stop killing games” proposal as a part of the DFA, though that may also be subject to change during the negotiation.In the end, I have a mixed opinion on much of this. I agree with most people that the scammy tactics some companies use really suck and make everyone’s life worse. But I’m skeptical you can legislate “fairness” broadly in a way that won’t backfire long term (see: cookie banners) or that takes into account all the edge cases. I’d prefer they target specific, proven, malicious behavior rather than writing sweeping rules.Part of the problem is that politicians can’t seem to think of the internet as anything more than Facebook, Instagram, X, and TikTok. To them, everything is social media, so anything that keeps you engaged must be “bad” and “addictive.” They legislate with that in mind, and when other services (Duolingo, Strava, etc.) push back, the fix is to make the rules “opt-out” rather than an outright ban. But that still puts compliance costs on those services, and it could also lead to some services never being built at all.A better solution, as always, is for people to have more overall control over their digital experiences, and I worry that laws like this could actually make that harder, because the compliance costs that giants can easily absorb can price out the smaller companies that are often the ones giving users more control in the first place. Small companies are already pointing out that this could really harm them, noting that the compliance costs are large, but they’re generally not the ones doing really scammy tactics in the first place. So to them, this would make them bear the cost, without much benefit to their users.Yes, giving users the option to turn off certain features would be a step towards more user control, which I appreciate, but the broadness of the law and the mandate makes me worry about how it will be gamed by the largest players, and prove too costly for the smaller ones.Indeed, we keep seeing big companies (and their lobbyists) shape these rules to benefit themselves long term, while leaving smaller competitors unable to comply.That is to say that I appreciate the underlying goals of this regulation, and agree that the state of the internet today often sucks. But that doesn’t mean that this regulation will actually make things any better — and there’s a decent enough chance it could make things worse.

item.title: Automakers Ramp Up Scare-Mongering Push To Ban Chinese EVs. You Know, ‘For Privacy’
item.author: Karl Bode
item.content:encoded: Automakers are aggressively ramping up their efforts to pass a new law outright banning Chinese EVs. They obviously want to do this because they don’t want to compete with better, often significantly cheaper products, but they can’t just that. Instead, we get a lot of bizarre pretense about how an industry with the worst privacy ratings in America is just super concerned about privacy. The auto industry’s preferred new law, the Connected Vehicle Security Act of 2026, cleared the Senate Commerce Committee in July, and a House version of the bill now has more than 100 co-sponsors. Last September, Senate bill sponsors, Sens. Bernie Moreno (a Republican) and Elissa Slotkin (a Democrat), agreed to delay efforts to fast-track the legislation until this month. “We need to ​protect the US market from a flood of Chinese imports that carry ​surveillance risk and disadvantage current manufacturers that have made generational investments in ⁠American communities.”This idea that Chinese EVs pose some unique privacy and national security threat to Americans is a common refrain from Bozzella and the auto industry. The argument is that Chinese EVs will collect oceans of data on American consumer driving and behavior habits, then funnel that data back to the Chinese government, who’ll then engage in all manner of ambiguous, nefarious behaviors. There are several problems with the argument. The biggest being that these same automakers do a disastrous job securing their own vehicles. Studies repeatedly show that U.S. automakers have some of the worst privacy and security standards in all of tech. An ocean of U.S. consumer driving, behavior, phone, and location data is already hoovered up at scale by your car, often left unencrypted, and sold to a laundry list of dodgy partners (including insurance companies, which will jack up your rates based on your driving habits with no transparency into the process).The other problem: the U.S. is routinely too corrupt to pass modern internet privacy laws or even competently regulate a vast international web of dodgy data brokers. Most of the data collected by U.S. vehicle makers is already available via these data brokers; who’ll in turn sell this data to literally any random nitwit with two nickels to rub together (including Chinese intelligence). Failing to secure your own vehicles and fighting tooth and nail against any privacy safeguards… then ranting incoherently about the threat of Chinese tech on U.S. shores is . Our failure to regulate data brokers or pass modern privacy laws means the Chinese simply buy this same data from any of dozens of dodgy companies already, making a lot of this stuff lazy pantomime.Democratic lawmakers in Michigan also recently tried to ban Chinese EVs from even visiting the state, suggesting that automakers are afraid of Americans cheaper overseas alternatives. The justification (by folks who are are, again, when it comes to any sort of domestic U.S. privacy standards and enforcement) is they were just very concerned about U.S. consumer privacy.I get the impulse to try and protect U.S. domestic automaker jobs (even though U.S. automakers have a long and detailed history of anti-labor behaviors), but there’s simply no coherent consistency to any U.S. policies. We don’t meaningfully protect labor generally, we don’t enforce consumer protection law, we’re too corrupt to pass a privacy law that reins in data monetization and hyper surveillance, and U.S. policymakers largely pay empty lip service to concepts like “affordability.”We’ll see how much the new Democratic blood in the House and Senate shifts some of these dynamics, but as it stands now you can expect the new year to be filled with the brim with all sorts of expanded bipartisan xenophobic protectionism across the entirety of tech — from AI to electric vehicles. Ignoring that it will be bumbling Trump zealots like Brendan Carr tasked with a lot of enforcement (see: Carr’s rank incompetence surrounding the Chinese drone ban). And you can expect all of it to be propped up by bad faith arguments that the bill backers are exclusively, suddenly, and very uncharacteristically concerned about your personal privacy. And in turn propped up by a shitty tech press oddly oblivious to their own nationalism biases. I maintain that the best path forward is to allow Chinese drones, AI, EVs, vacuums, and assorted other tech into the U.S. market, but properly fund, staff, and legally support our privacy, labor, competition, and consumer protection regulators to ensure a level playing field and healthy markets. Large corporations hate that idea, so instead we get this bizarre and performative protectionist pantomime.

item.title: 'Java4Shell' Flaw Exposes OpenJDK to RCE via Base64
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Longtime Slashdot reader HnT writes: Security researchers at Calif have disclosed Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a critical 9.2-rated memory-corruption bug in OpenJDK's AVX-512 Base64 decoder. By sending a malformed string ending in a stray = character, attackers can trigger an out-of-bounds heap write to leak sensitive memory or achieve pre-auth remote code execution on major platforms like Jira, Jenkins, and Keycloak. Although Calif says the vulnerability is difficult to exploit, Oracle released a critical patch update Tuesday, and CISA urged organizations to update immediately. OpenJDK's security advisory can be found here.
The Calif researchers warned that vulnerable systems could remain exposed for five to 10 years, given how slowly some organizations patch their infrastructure.

item.title: NYC Mayor Mamdani Disbands NYPD Unit That Treated Protesters Like Terrorists
item.author: Tim Cushing
item.content:encoded: It’s taken pretty much forever, but finally one of the NYPD’s worst specialist units is being disbanded. The catalyst here was the election of a mayor who was finally serious about holding the NYPD in check. For years, the city’s mayors have done whatever they can to keep the cop shop happy, including the last mayor, who went deep down a corruption hole to make sure both he NYPD remained happy, even if his constituents weren’t. A controversial New York Police Department unit accused of using excessive force against protesters has been disbanded, Mayor Zohran Mamdani and NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch announced Monday, fulfilling a key campaign promise from the mayor to separate protest policing from counterterrorism.Along with the elimination of the Strategic Response Group, certain aggressive crowd-management tactics are now banned and new dialogue-focused units will be established in the NYPD and the Mayor’s Office of Community Safety to ensure a coordinated response to protests, the mayor and commissioner said in a statement.If you’re wondering about the controversy of this particular unit, you have to take a trip in the wayback machine to 2015, which was when NYPD Commissioner and the mayor who never was the reformer he pretended to be (Bill de Blasio) decided a single unit could handle three very different aspects of policing, somehow without causing collateral damage to Constitutional rights. (Or maybe they didn’t actually belive this and chose to do it anyway.) The SRG got folded in with an existing counterterrorism unit, apparently because the mayor and police commissioner decided fighting terrorism and policing protests was roughly the same thing. A few years later, documents obtained by journalists made it clear SRG officers were routinely brutalizing peaceful protesters. This wasn’t much of a surprise, considering its counterterrorism unit was known for routinely violating rights while engaging in extremely biased policing/surveillance. That this infection would spread to the SRG is completely unsurprising. Bad apples, etc. This unit should have been disbanded once this information was made public. But it wasn’t. Given that regular NYPD patrol officers are just as capable of violating people’s rights, it hardly made sense to provide specialist pay for rote thuggery. But the SRG kept on keeping on… right up until NYC residents made it explicitly clear they were sick of the same old bullshit from their mayors. The disbanding of this unit has the support of the current police commissioner. And it goes further than just rearranging some deck chairs so SRG officers can get back to the rights-violation business elsewhere. It also establishes a “First Amendment Support Team” in the NYPD that will help train and support officers who are asked to police protests. In addition, “kettling” protesters is no longer an option. The popular — and extremely abusive — tactic is used by plenty of PDs around the nation. Under the guise of breaking up a demonstration, officers surround protesters, physically force them into a confined area, and then rain down pepper balls and tear gas on protesters whose only other option is to physically force their way out of the “kettle.” This, of course, leads to even more police violence, as well as trumped-up “assaulting an officer” charges as people try to escape this form of mass imprisonment. The dissolution order also says this, which is pretty fucking wild: [T]he use of bicycles as weapons will be allowed only when preventing death or physical injury to an officer or another person.[If you haven’t watched the Prime series “Patriot,” you’re only hurting yourself.]You can’t reform a unit that has been given the greenlight to be as awful as it can be for nearly a decade. The only fix is shutting it down and starting over with an emphasis on making officers realize that people’s rights are just as important as their safety. If this leads to more officers resigning or retiring because they don’t want to work for an employer that expects them to respect the law… GOOD. New York City residents are better off without them.

item.title: Our Dipshit DHS Secretary’s Outage Expert: “One Guy That’s Very Smart With Tech”
item.author: Mike Masnick
item.content:encoded: It should be no surprise that people are also connecting the dots and wondering if these things are all connected. I mean, how could you not? For what it’s worth, I tend to agree with the experts Prof. Kate Klonick has spoken to who suggest the explanation is a benign one — old systems do break down, and it can be a bit of a coincidence that a bunch of big-name systems all broke down around the same time, but humans (as pattern-matching animals) are just paying closer attention to all of them breaking down at once.WHY IS EVERYTHING BREAKING? A thread on the internet suddenly going to hell So in 5 days, Outlook went down, US air traffic control went down, banking systems went down, NSA confidential telephone systems go down and just now that Apple services are downWTAF is happening?!?!1/If there is a throughline here, my is that a lot of the tech companies have been quick to push layoffs lately, stupidly believing that they can replace people with AI (which, as we’ve been saying, is a dumb plan), and that means a lot of expertise — including the kind of tacit knowledge AI can’t easily capture — has walked out the door. When the people who actually know how to keep these old systems running are gone, those systems become a bit more likely to fail. That is, while lots of people jumped to “AI” being to blame, my guess (and it is a guess) is that it’s less the direct impact of AI systems, and much more the downstream indirect results of stupid CEOs cutting corners by laying off the kind of people who could keep these systems online.Still, it does no one any favors to have the dumbest fucking people alive in charge of all of this, but we do. Back on Friday when the FAA ground stop situation happened, the first one to talk about it was DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin (who, back when he was a senator, was long considered one of the dumbest people in the Senate). When asked if the FAA situations had anything to do with AI he responded by refusing to rule it out (“You just can’t rule out anything at this point”) and with the absolutely ridiculous retort: “We call it SI around here, remember?” He also said that it wasn’t “another 9/11” which is an awfully odd comparison to make, and only served to make many people wonder if we should be even more worried.Later that evening he appeared next to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, where there were awkward exchanges where Duffy and Mullin didn’t appear to be on the same page about what happened or what was to blame. However, both the FAA and the contractor behind its newly expanded $875 million AI system insisted that system had nothing to do with it.Then, on Monday evening Mullin went on Sean Hannity’s show and… reminded everyone just how clueless he still is. The video clips are remarkable, mainly this one that shows him first suggesting that all the outages don’t appear to be a cyberattack, based on his conversations with CISA, and then saying how he spoke to some successful tech bro who he says asked not to be named (though he says it’s not Elon) who fed him some nonsense that, once it makes it through the empty caverns of Mullin’s brain, came out even more garbled:It's one thing to watch two random guys bullshitting about what's behind the tech outages. We're all used to that on TV.But this is literally the SECRETARY OF HOMELAND SECURITY just wildly speculating. This dude is supposed to be following the facts and actually figuring it out right now.Mullin mentions that he had the folks at CISA (the Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency) look into all of these events, and they told him that it doesn’t appear to be an interrelated cyberattack.“[W]hen we start looking at the cyber world, I start asking CISA, hey, what’s going on here? And they said, sir, we’re not seeing any traffic that would make us think that this is a cyberattack, they’re all individually unrelated.”Yes, that’s right, the federal government gutted its cybersecurity infrastructure staff and put many of those who remained on “deportation paperwork processing” instead. And that hollowed-out agency is the one we’re now relying on to tell us everything’s fine.Anyway, the next bit of Mullin’s ramblings to Hannity is just absolutely bizarre:“And so I started talking to the tech industry, and one guy that’s very smart with tech…it’s not Elon…I said, what could be causing all these separate outages, and he says, I believe that it’s the SI. He said because these programs aren’t designed to work as fast as SI is, and so, when they…put in a program that’s able to write codes, and it goes in, it self-fixes itself, as it starts self-fixing itself, it’s like doing a change order on a house. When you change one thing in a house, everything else starts changing, and it’s a ripple effect, and it causes these systems to be over[run] that weren’t designed to run as fast as the SI technology is today. That was the conversation I had today. That kind of makes sense to me.”Sooooooo… you can kinda piece together what someone probably told Mullin if we backtrack it through the reverse-stupid filter. From Mullin’s description, it sounds like someone explained to him what recursive self-improvement (RSI) means (“self-fixing”) and he then tried to apply that to the outages? Except that RSI is on the training new models side of things, not the keeping basic infrastructure working side of things. The whole “work as fast as” and “self-fixing” thing really sounds very much like someone who was told a few things about how AI systems work and are trained and not understanding the technology even slightly, and regurgitating it to the press in the stupidest way possible.Also, dude, you’re the Secretary of Homeland Security, speaking to “one guy that’s very smart with tech” is not exactly the way you should be going around trying to get a handle on what’s happening with our technology systems these days.As mentioned, it’s very possible AI played an indirect role here, and some of these outages may even have more direct AI-related causes. item.title: Jensen Huang's Fall Hits 'Open' Models In Boost to Anthropic and OpenAI
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia could weaken the open AI model ecosystem he spent years championing, potentially strengthening closed-model developers like OpenAI and Anthropic, according to the Financial Times. From the report: The US chip giant's former chief threw Nvidia's balance sheet into creating a broad AI ecosystem, including by seeding and acquiring start-ups involved in the development of open-source and open-weight models, which users can customize and run on their own hardware. Huang was a forceful advocate for their spread, lobbying against Washington's moves to restrict the use of Chinese-made open models while seeking the development of US alternatives. "Our AI leadership will be judged not by one frontier AI model, but by whether the United States builds a strong, open ecosystem that diffuses into every sector," he wrote this summer in his first-ever message on X.
His ignominious exit from Nvidia deprives the open model sector of its most vocal and influential supporter in the US. "I think Jensen stood to gain the most economically and was personally committed to diversity at the model layer," said one venture capitalist who has invested in AI start-ups alongside Nvidia. "Without him and a less generous Nvidia in terms of investment, we may end up in a much more concentrated world of model providers."
Whether Nvidia will continue the rapid pace of dealmaking under a new leader is unclear. The company was expected to participate in or lead four start-up deals currently under discussion: investments in Thinking Machines Lab and Groq, a potential partnership with Reflection AI and the $12.9bn acquisition of open model repository Hugging Face. "Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia, but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract," said Elon Musk in a post on X on Saturday. "Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost."
"In some sense [Huang leaving Nvidia] is bad for the industry, but in some sense Jensen is an enemy of the frontier labs because he wants models to become commoditized so he retains the prime position in the value chain," said one senior figure at a leading Silicon Valley AI company.
"I don't think open weight models are going away... but losing Jensen as their greatest financial backer and champion will slow their progress, and I imagine will not hurt Anthropic's IPO," said another industry figure.
"It's reasonable to expect the ouster of Jensen will concentrate computing power more in the hands of frontier labs and hyperscalers," added a senior figure at an AI lab. "That's good for the labs."
